column2: There are thousands of other rivers, holy, auspicious, and bearing cool waters, which are replenished wherever Indra showers down rain.
It is impossible to recount the names or even the dimensions of those holy and excellent rivers.
The joyous people of those lands ever drink of those rivers; that dvipa, abounding in milk, is shaped like a discus.
It is overspread with the waters of rivers and with mountains resembling clouds, rich in manifold minerals and embellished with gems and coral.
It is filled with diverse cities and flourishing provinces, with trees laden with flowers and fruits, and it abounds everywhere in wealth and grain.
It is encompassed on all sides by the ocean of milk, which is coextensive with Shaka-dvipa all around.
Within it are holy provinces, mountains, and auspicious rivers; those seven lands are remembered as fully furnished with the four castes and stages of life.
There is no intermixture of castes and stages of life anywhere among them; and since righteousness is never transgressed, the people enjoy unbroken happiness.
Whence could greed, deceit, malice, or envy arise among them? There is no inversion of the natural order of time in that land.
There is no exaction of taxes, no punishment, and none deserving punishment; knowing dharma, they protect one another by means of their own duty alone.
Thus much alone can be declared regarding that dvipa; thus much alone is to be heard concerning the inhabitants of Shaka-dvipa.
I shall now describe Pushkara, the seventh dvipa; listen. The ocean of milk is encompassed on the outside by Pushkara-dvipa.
It is twice as extensive as Shaka-dvipa on every side. In Pushkara there is but a single glorious mountain, a mighty mass of rock,
uplifted with variegated peaks made of gems and with clusters of crags; the great mountain of many-coloured ridges stands in the eastern half of that dvipa.
It extends for twenty-five thousand yojanas across, and rises thirty-four thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth.
The mountain Manasottara is cast around the half of the dvipa; standing near the shore, it rises aloft like the new moon.
It is raised fifty thousand yojanas upward and is equally broad, perfectly circular on every side.
That same earth-bearing mountain Manasa stands also in the western half of the dvipa; though a single great mass, its circuit is disposed in two portions.
It is encompassed on all sides by the ocean of sweet water, which extends everywhere to the same measure as Pushkara-dvipa.
In that dvipa two holy and auspicious regions are remembered, lying in the zones on either side of the mountain Manasa.
The region outside Manasa is the varsha named Mahavita, and that which lies within it is called Dhataki-khanda.
Men there live for ten thousand years, free from sickness and full of happiness, endowed with the perfection that is born of the mind.
In those two varshas the span of life and the comeliness of form are the same for all; there are none inferior or superior among them, for they are equal in beauty and in character.
There is no robber there, no deceiver, no jealousy, malice, or fear; there is neither restraint nor punishment, neither greed nor hoarding of possessions.
There is neither truth nor falsehood there, nor righteousness and unrighteousness; neither castes and stages of life, nor agriculture, cattle-tending, or the merchant's trade.
The threefold Veda, the science of chastisement, service, and the crafts — all these do not exist in the two varshas of Pushkara.
There is no rainfall there, nor rivers, nor cold and heat; there are no plants springing from the ground, nor waters descending from mountain torrents.
The people there have a span of life equal to that of the Uttara Kurus; they are happy in every season and untouched by the onset of old age.
Thus has the entire arrangement of Pushkara been proclaimed in due order, in Dhataki-khanda as well as in Mahavita.
Pushkara is encompassed by the ocean of sweet water, equal in extent to the full circuit of Pushkara itself.
Thus the seven dvipas are encircled by the seven oceans; the ocean that comes after each dvipa is equal in extent to that dvipa.
Thus should the successive enlargement of the dvipas and the oceans be understood; and because it is replete with waters, the sea is named samudra.
Because the fourfold classes of beings enter and dwell within it, it is called a varsha, since it bestows happiness upon the people.
It is called varsha also in the sense of delight and the exercise of procreative vigour, for it fosters the pleasures of love among those who abide therein.
In the bright fortnight the ocean ever fills as the moon waxes; when the moon wanes in the dark fortnight, the waters diminish as the luminary declines.
The ocean, when it fills, is filled of itself; and when it wanes, it is drawn back into itself alone.
Just as water placed in a pot upon the fire is seen to swell up through contact with the flame, so the water within the great ocean increases of itself.
Without any real loss or excess, the waters wax and wane with the rising and setting of the moon in the bright and dark fortnights.
The increase and decrease of the ocean follow the waxing and waning of the moon, to the measure of five hundred and ten finger-breadths.

The rise and fall of the ocean's waters are observed on the days of the full and new moon; and the dvipas are so called because water lies on both sides of them, for they are everywhere surrounded by water.
Since it is the resting-place of waters, the ocean is called udadhi; hills are without joints or ridges, while mountains are named parvatas after their jointed crests.
In Plaksha-dvipa stands the mountain Gomeda, from which the land takes its renown; in Shalmala-dvipa the Shalmali tree is worshipped by men of great vows.
In Kusha-dvipa there is a clump of Kusha grass, and by its name that dvipa is called; in Krauncha-dvipa stands the mountain Krauncha in the midst of the land.
In Shaka-dvipa stands the Shaka tree, and by its name the dvipa is called; in Pushkara-dvipa stands the banyan tree, reverently saluted by those who dwell there.
There Mahadeva worships Brahma, the lord of the three worlds; Brahma, the lord of creatures, dwells in that land together with the Sadhyas.
The thirty-three gods, together with the great sages, worship him there; he is adored as the most excellent among the excellent gods.
From Jambu-dvipa onward, the manifold excellences of the people proceed and increase in due order in all those dvipas;
by reason of their continence, truthfulness, and self-restraint, their health and the measure of their life are doubled in each succeeding dvipa.
In this Pushkara-dvipa, the Self-born One himself protects the people dwelling in the two varshas that have been mentioned, O learned sages.
The Lord, uplifting his staff of chastisement, is Brahma, the lord of the three worlds; he is the minister of the god Vishnu, he is the father, and he is the grandsire of all.
And food of six flavours, exceedingly invigorating, presents itself there of its own accord, without any effort; the subjects partake of it always.
Beyond Pushkara stands the great ocean of sweet water, Svadudaka, encompassing it all around on every side.
Beyond it is seen the great expanse where the worlds are established; there lies a golden land, twice as large, everywhere like a single slab of rock.
Beyond that land is a mountain of circular extent, partly luminous and partly dark; it is called Lokaloka, the boundary of the world and the region beyond.
On the side facing the worlds there is light, and beyond it lies the lightless region; its height is remembered as ten thousand yojanas.
Its breadth upon the earth is the same, and it moves at will; the luminous portion abides within the sphere of the worlds, while the lightless portion is otherworldly.
The worlds are measured to its inner half, and the lightless region lies outside; the Aloka region extends all around beyond, equal in extent to the expanse of the worlds.
It is bounded on all sides and enveloped by water; and beyond Aloka, the cosmic Egg stands enclosing everything.
Within the Egg are these worlds and the earth with its seven continents — Bhurloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Maharloka likewise.
Janaloka, Tapoloka and Satyaloka — this is the entire collection of the worlds; this much alone is to be known, and whatever is beyond is the utmost limit of the worlds.
As the moon stands in the western quarter at the beginning of the bright fortnight, such is the shape of the Egg.
Of such Eggs there are known to be crores upon thousands, extending horizontally, above and below, belonging to the Cause, the imperishable Self.
Each Egg is enveloped by seven natural sheaths, each exceeding the one within it tenfold, and they mutually sustain one another.
All of them are mutually enveloped and mutually produced; and all around this Egg is established the ocean of dense water.
The Egg stands sustained on all sides by those dense waters; beyond the dense mass, its sphere extends horizontally and upward.
That sphere of water stands sustained all around by fiery energy; the fire is like a ball of iron, spherical in form on every side.
It stands sustained all around by the dense wind; and the ether, in like manner, supports the dense wind.
Bhutadi, the principle of ego, supports the ether, and Mahat, the great principle, supports Bhutadi; and Mahat is sustained by the infinite, the unmanifest.
That infinite, unmanifest one is subtle in ten ways, endless, self-existent, without beginning and without end.
Beyond it, it is terrible, supportless, and free from all affliction, removed by many thousands of yojanas and enveloped by nothing.
It is darkness itself, lightless, boundless, without divisions of space, unknown even to the gods, and devoid of all activity.
It is renowned as lying at the end of darkness and at the end of ether, lustreless — the great abode of the infinite Lord at His boundary.
That divine region is inaccessible even to the thirty-three gods — so declares the sacred tradition; it is the fixed boundary of the great Lord of lords.
The worlds celebrated by the wise as extending up to the moon and the sun are called the Lokas, and they constitute the universe, without doubt.
The seven nether regions beginning with Rasatala and the seven upper worlds, the seven courses of the wind, together with the abode of Brahma, O twice-born ones —
from Patala up to heaven, within this range moves the fivefold course of beings; this is the measure of the universe, this ocean of worldly existence.
Creatures born of many species wander through it endlessly, without beginning; such is the wonderful Prakriti of Brahman, established in the universe.
Whatever is divine here, or of nature, its vast extent is not perceived even by the illustrious Siddhas who have transcended the senses.
Of earth, water, fire, wind, ether and darkness, and of the cosmic body of the infinite Lord, O best of the twice-born —
there is no decay, no transformation, and no end whatsoever; He is infinite everywhere, and thus it is recited in the scriptures of knowledge.
Of Him I have spoken already, in the recitation of His names, where He who bears the name Padmanabha, the lotus-navelled one, has been glorified in full.
He alone is present everywhere and is worshipped in all regions — on the earth and in Rasatala, in the ether, in the wind, and in fire.
In all the oceans and in heaven likewise, without doubt, and in the darkness too, this one of great splendour alone is to be known.
The great Yogin Janardana, whose limbs are apportioned in many ways, the Lord of all worlds, the mighty one, is worshipped in manifold forms in every world.
Thus mutually produced, they are mutually sustained in the relation of supporter and supported; they are modifications, yet themselves unmodified.
Earth and the other elements are modifications, mutually bounded, each exceeding the other, and mutually interpenetrating.
Because they are mutually produced, they have attained stability; formerly they were without distinction, and distinction arose from mutual specification.
The elements beginning with earth are delimited from one another; their delimitation is determined in particular by the accumulation of their qualities.
The delimitation of the rest is not conceived here owing to their subtlety; beyond the elements, that which extends is remembered as the supporting expanse.
The elements are everywhere delimited within the ether, just as smaller vessels are contained within a great vessel.
They exist deficient in one another, through mutual dependence; so too, the divisions within the ether are held to be contained one within another.
All these four are each greater than the preceding; so long as these elements exist, so long is production said to take place.
Like the interweaving of threads in a fabric, their mutual penetration within the elements is held to be; apart from the elements, the production of effects does not exist.

Therefore the differentiated entities, being of the nature of effects, are held to be limited; and those divisions which are of the nature of causes, such as Mahat and the rest, are similarly reckoned.
Thus has this arrangement been declared by me in detail, O twice-born ones — the Egg with its seven continents and oceans, exactly as it truly is.
In extent and in detail, by enumeration, this is but a partial account of the transformations of Him whose principal form is the universe itself.
All this universe is presided over by the Lord; thus the seven groups of constituents are established, mutually interpenetrating.
This much of the arrangement I have been able to describe; this much alone is to be heard regarding the disposition of the universe, O king.
But these seven Prakritis mutually sustain one another; their measure I cannot venture to reckon here.
The Prakritis are innumerable, extending horizontally, upward and downward; and so too is the arrangement of the stars, reaching as far as the divine celestial sphere.
Thus has been described, in due order, the arrangement of the earth and the sphere that follows it. Now, O discerning ones, I shall set forth what lies above the earth.
The goddess Earth is covered with many countries, many capitals and cities, many rivers, streams and mountains, and is thronged with creatures of many kinds.
The divine Earth, of vast extent, is sung of as endless, with beings dwelling in her rivers, streams and oceans, and those abiding in humble abodes.
And those stationed in the mountains and the sky, and those gone within the earth — the waters are to be known as endless, and so too is fire, which moves through all the worlds.
Fire is proclaimed endless, all-pervading, the source of all things; likewise ether is remembered as boundless, lovely, and the support of many.
Wind also, born of ether, is proclaimed endless. The earth is established upon the waters, and the waters are stationed above the earth.
Beyond them is ether; then again earth, and again water. Thus no limit of this endless material creation is ever found.
And know that the earths are heaped up one upon another; whatever succession there is — earth, water, then ether.
This arrangement is well known in these seven netherworlds; each earthly realm of Rasatala extends ten thousand yojanas.
Thus has the extent of each been reckoned by the wise. The first is named Atala, and beyond that is Sutala.
Then one should know Talatala, the realm of vast extent; below that is the region named Mahatala, and beyond it Rasatala.
And in the part below all these, Patala is remembered as the seventh. The first region of the nether earth is declared to be of black soil.
The second has white soil, the third blue clay, the fourth yellow soil, and the fifth is made of gravel.
The sixth is known as made of rock, and the seventh is remembered as golden. In this first realm is famed the palace of the king of the Asuras.
The abode of Namuci, of Indrashatru and of Mahanada; the city of Shankukarna and the palace of Kabandha.
The city of Nishkulada, filled with joyful people; and the abode of the terrible Rakshasa Shuladanta.
The city of Lohitaksha and of Kalinga, and of Shvapada; and the city of the noble Naga lord Dhananjaya.
The city of the Naga Kaliya and of Kaushika. In this manner are the thousands of cities of the Nagas, Danavas and Rakshasas.
These are to be known in the first realm of black soil, without doubt. In the second realm, Sutala, O Brahmanas, are the cities of the lord of the Daityas and of the Rakshasas.
The city of Mahajambha, and likewise of the foremost one; the palace of Hayagriva, of Krishna, and of Nikumbha.
The city of the Daitya named Shankha and of Gomukha; and of the Rakshasas Nila, Megha and Kathana.
The abode of Kukupada and the abode of Mahoshnisha; the city of the Naga Kambala and of Ashvatara.
And the city of Kadru's son, the noble Takshaka. In this manner are the thousands of cities of the Nagas, Danavas and Rakshasas.
These are in this second realm of white soil, O Brahmanas, without doubt. In the third realm is famed the city of the noble Prahlada.
The city of Anuhrada, the city of Agnimukha, the city of Taraka, and likewise the city of Trishiras.
The city of Shishumara and the city of Tripura; and that of the Daitya Puranjana, thronged with joyous and well-nourished people.
And to be known is the palace of the Rakshasa Cyavana; and the city of the Rakshasa lords Kumbhila and Khara.
And the city of the cruel Viradha and of Ulkamukha; of the Naga Hemaka and of Panduraka.
The city of Maninaga and the palace of Kapila; the palace of the serpent lord Nedaka and of Vishalaksha.
In this manner are the thousands of cities of the Nagas, Danavas and Rakshasas in this third realm of blue soil, O Brahmanas, without doubt.
In the fourth realm is the city of the lion among Daityas, the noble Kalanemi; the city of Gajakarna and the city of Kunjara.
And the vast city of the Rakshasa lord Sumali; the abode of Munja, the lord of the world, and of Vrikavaktra.
The city of Vainateya, extending many yojanas and thronged with many birds, is in this fourth netherworld.
In the fifth realm of gravelly soil, extending many yojanas, is the city of the wise lion of Daityas, Virocana.
The abodes of Vaidyuta, of Agnijihva and of Hiranyaksha; and the city of the wise Rakshasa lord Vidyujjihva.
The city of Sahamegha and of the Rakshasa lord Mali; and of the Nagas Kirmira, Svastika and Jaya.
In this manner the thousands of cities of the Nagas, Danavas and Rakshasas are ever to be known in this fifth realm, the heap of gravel.
In the sixth realm is the excellent city of the Daitya lord Kesarin; and the city of Suparvan, of Puloman and of Mahisha.
And the city of the noble Rakshasa lord Surosha. There dwells, full of joy, the hundred-headed son of Surasa.
The glorious Naga king named Vasuki, the friend of Mahendra. In this manner are the thousands of cities of the Nagas, Danavas and Rakshasas.
These are famed in this sixth realm of rocky soil, Rasatala. In the seventh realm, Patala, the last of all, is to be known.
The joyous city of Bali, thronged with crowds of men and women, full of Asuras and venomous serpents and of delighted foes of the gods.
And there itself is the great city of the Daitya Mucukunda, together with many lofty great cities of the sons of Diti.
And likewise with splendid cities of the Nagas by the thousand, and with the lofty great cities of the Daityas and the Danavas.
It is thronged with many lofty dwellings of the Rakshasas. And at the end of Patala, O best of Brahmanas, in a region many yojanas wide,
dwells the noble one whose eyes are like red lotuses, unaging and immortal, whose belly is like a polished conch, clad in dark-blue garments, of great might.
Broad of hood, lustrous, wearing variegated garlands and powerful, he shines with his white golden crests and his glowing face.
The lord shines with his thousand faces, wearing a single earring; he blazes with the garland of his tongues, like flames of flickering fire.
Encircled by a garland of flames, he appears like mount Kailasa; and he shines with his full two thousand eyes,
reddened like the morning sun, his body glossy and pale white; of him whose hue is like the jasmine flower and the moon, the row of eyes shines resplendent.
